message.content:
The salt air bit at Elias’s cheeks, a familiar sting that had become the rhythm of his life. For thirty years, he had stood watch atop the Blackwood Light, a solitary sentinel against the relentless Atlantic. The lighthouse was not just a structure; it was a living entity, its gears groaning in the wind, its lens rotating with a hypnotic, eternal grace.

Tonight, the storm was particularly vicious. Waves crashed against the jagged rocks below, sending sprays of freezing foam high enough to lick the gallery railing. Inside the lantern room, the great Fresnel lens spun, casting its powerful beam through the driving rain. Elias adjusted the wick, his hands rough and calloused, moving with the muscle memory of decades. He knew every creak of the iron stairs, every draft that slipped through the window frames.

A radio crackle broke the silence. It was the coast guard, reporting a distress signal from a small fishing trawler struggling near the reef. Elias looked out into the black void. The beam swept across the churning water, a golden sword cutting through the darkness. He saw nothing but chaos. He tightened his grip on the railing, feeling the vibration of the tower beneath his feet. He was the only thing standing
